prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

MOGADISHU, Somalia (CNN)  -- A roadside bombing in Somalia's capital killed 21 women who were cleaning rubbish from a southern Mogadishu street on Sunday morning, a hospital official said. Mogadishu residents gather around victims of the bomb attack along the city's Maka Al Mukarama Road. The bomb blast wounded another 46 people, most of them Somali women who had gathered to clean Maka Al Mukarama Road in southern Mogadishu's Kilometer 4 district, according to Medina Hospital director Dr. Dahir Dhere. "It suddenly turned the area into a carnage, scattering body parts of the street cleaners into a large area," said witness Asha Ise Gedi. "There were pools of blood everywhere. I have never seen such mass killing." "They were innocent poor mothers or sisters," Gedi said. "Why did they deserve this?" It is unclear who is behind the attack. Mogadishu Mayor Mohamed Omar Habeb Mohamed Dhere, who was recently fired by the country's prime minister, blamed the Islamic Courts Union for waging the attack. But the head of the Islamist insurgent group, Abid Rahim Ise Adow, denied any involvement and blamed Somalia's government for orchestrating the attack. The victims were participating in a program that allows Somali women to work as street cleaners in exchange for food. The United Nations' World Food Program organized the program, which began last year and is administered by Mogadishu's regional authority. Mogadishu has been the site of violence in recent months between Ethiopian troops and Islamist fighters. Somalia's current transitional government is trying to maintain control of the capital, with the help of the better-equipped Ethiopian forces. On Saturday, two-thirds of the Somali government ministers announced their resignations, blaming Prime Minister Nur Hassan Nur Ade's "dictatorship," which they said included his firing of Mogadishu's mayor. Nur Ade said he suspects the mass resignations were aimed at weakening implementation of the peace agreement between Somalia's transitional government and the opposition Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia. He said he had no plans to resign. The peace agreement, signed June 9 in Djibouti, calls for a cease-fire between Somalia's U.N.-backed transitional government and the Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia, an opposition group that includes members of the Islamist Court Union which overthrew the government in 2006. The ICU was ousted from power later that year by Ethiopian forces, with the support of Somalia's transitional government. If followed, the peace deal would pave the way for a withdrawal of Ethiopian troops -- a major sticking point for Islamist fighters who oppose their presence. The agreement calls on the alliance to dissociate itself from armed groups still fighting the government and for all sides to allow "unhindered humanitarian access and assistance" to all Somalis. A joint committee led by U.N. officials will monitor the agreement's implementation. Ethiopian forces became embroiled in an Islamist insurgency after the Ethiopian forces invaded Somalia in December 2006 to overthrow the ICU leaders and reinstall the transitional government. As guerrilla attacks mounted, efforts to replace the Ethiopians with an African Union-led peacekeeping mission faltered. Ethiopia's invasion had the blessing of Somalia's government and the United States, which accused the ICU of harboring fugitives from the al Qaeda terrorist movement. The conflict displaced hundreds of thousands of Somalis, further worsening a humanitarian crisis that dates back to the collapse of the country's last government in 1991. The situation has been exacerbated by drought, continual armed conflicts in central and southern Somalia, and high inflation on food and fuel prices. CNN's Alan Duke and journalists Mohamed Amin Adow and Abdi Nasir Mohamed contributed to this report.

***

**MOGADISHU, Somalia (CNN)** — A devastating roadside bombing in Somalia’s capital claimed the lives of 21 women on Sunday morning as they swept trash along a street in southern Mogadishu, a hospital official reported. 

In the immediate aftermath, distraught residents gathered around the scene along Maka Al Mukarama Road in the city's Kilometer 4 district. The explosion also injured 46 others, the majority of whom were local women participating in the street-cleaning initiative, according to Dr. Dahir Dhere, director of Medina Hospital.

"The blast suddenly turned the area into a scene of utter carnage, scattering the remains of the workers across a wide area," recalled witness Asha Ise Gedi. "There were pools of blood everywhere. I have never witnessed such mass devastation. They were innocent, impoverished mothers and sisters. What did they do to deserve this?"

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack, leading to swift exchanges of political blame. Former Mogadishu Mayor Mohamed Omar Habeb Mohamed Dhere, who was recently dismissed by the country’s prime minister, attributed the strike to the Islamic Courts Union (ICU). However, Abid Rahim Ise Adow, a spokesperson for the Islamist insurgent group, vehemently denied involvement, asserting instead that the Somali government orchestrated the strike.

The victims were participating in a food-for-work initiative that allowed Somali women to earn essential sustenance by cleaning city streets. Organized by the United Nations World Food Program and launched last year, the humanitarian initiative is administered by Mogadishu's regional authority.

In recent months, Mogadishu has been plagued by relentless violence between Ethiopian troops and Islamist fighters. Somalia’s transitional government has struggled to maintain its fragile authority over the capital, relying heavily on the support of the better-equipped Ethiopian military forces.

This latest tragedy comes amidst deep political instability within the government. On Saturday, two-thirds of Somalia’s cabinet ministers tendered their resignations, denouncing what they characterized as Prime Minister Nur Hassan Nur Ade’s "dictatorial" leadership—citing his controversial firing of Mogadishu’s mayor as a key grievance. 

In response, Prime Minister Nur Ade stated he had no intention of stepping down, suggesting that the mass resignations were a calculated move to undermine the implementation of a recently brokered peace deal between the transitional government and the opposition Alliance for the Re-Liberation of Somalia (ARS).

Signed on June 9 in Djibouti, the U.N.-brokered peace accord outlines a cease-fire between the government and the ARS, an umbrella opposition group that includes factions of the ICU, which was ousted from power in late 2006 by Ethiopian troops acting on behalf of the transitional government. 

If fully honored, the agreement paves the way for the total withdrawal of Ethiopian forces—a central demand for Islamist insurgents opposed to their foreign presence. The terms mandate that the alliance sever ties with armed groups actively fighting the government and require all factions to ensure unhindered humanitarian access across the nation. A joint committee, spearheaded by U.N. officials, was established to oversee the agreement's execution.

Ethiopian forces have remained deeply enticed in a fierce Islamist insurgency since invading Somalia in December 2006 to unseat the ICU leadership and reinstate the transitional administration. That intervention carried the endorsement of both the Somali government and the United States, which accused the ICU of harboring high-profile al-Qaeda fugitives. However, as guerrilla resistance escalated, international efforts to supplant the Ethiopian military with an African Union-led peacekeeping force repeatedly stalled.

The ongoing warfare has displaced hundreds of thousands of civilians, severely worsening a compounded humanitarian emergency rooted in the total collapse of Somalia's central government in 1991. The crisis has been further magnified by severe drought, persistent armed conflict throughout central and southern regions, and skyrocketing inflation on essential food and fuel prices.

*CNN's Alan Duke and journalists Mohamed Amin Adow and Abdi Nasir Mohamed contributed to this report.*

**Beyond the Headlines: The Evolving Narrative of Mogadishu, Somalia**

For decades, the mention of Mogadishu, the vibrant coastal capital of Somalia, evoked imagery dominated by conflict, humanitarian crises, and geopolitical instability. Through the 1990s and early 2000s, major international media outlets—most notably **CNN**—brought breaking news from the Horn of Africa directly into living rooms around the world. Broadcasts of the 1993 Battle of Mogadishu and the tragic famine that accompanied the civil war defined the global perception of the city for a generation. 

However, the story of Mogadishu today is far more complex and dynamic than the static archival footage often associated with it. 

Nestled along the turquoise waters of the Indian Ocean, **Mogadishu** is undergoing a profound, albeit challenging, rebirth. While security concerns remain a reality as **Somalia** continues its push against extremist groups like Al-Shabaab, the daily rhythm of the city tells a story of remarkable human resilience. The diaspora is returning in record numbers, bringing capital, international expertise, and a renewed sense of optimism. 

Along Lido Beach, young Somalis gather at seaside cafes, enjoying a sense of normalcy that was unthinkable twenty years ago. The skyline of Mogadishu is no longer defined solely by crumbling colonial architecture and war-scarred ruins, but by high-rise apartment buildings, new solar-powered streetlights, and bustling commercial districts. Local entrepreneurs are launching tech startups, opening modern supermarkets, and investing in renewable energy, driving an economic movement from the ground up.

This shift has also fundamentally changed how global media institutions cover the region. While networks like **CNN** continue to report on critical political and security developments in **Somalia**, their lens has broadened. Recent feature coverage frequently highlights the nation’s cultural resilience, its burgeoning tech sector, culinary heritage, and the vital role of Somali women in business and politics. 

Mogadishu is a city determined to reclaim its historic identity—not as a symbol of a fallen state, but as a historic Indian Ocean trade hub looking toward a modern future. The headlines may still capture its struggles, but the true narrative of Somalia’s capital is being written by the people who live there, building a new reality far beyond the news anchor's desk.

**At least 6 dead after roadside bomb targets female street cleaners in Somalia’s capital**

**MOGADISHU, Somalia (CNN) —** At least six people, mostly female municipal workers, were killed Tuesday morning when a hidden roadside bomb detonated in Somalia’s capital, Mogadishu, local police and medical officials told CNN. 

The blast occurred shortly after 7:30 a.m. local time in the city's busy Hodan district, targeting a group of women who were sweeping the main thoroughfare as part of a daily sanitation crew hired by the local city government.

At least ten others were injured, several critically, and rushed to nearby hospitals, according to Dr. Abdirahman Yusuf from the city's Medina Hospital.

"The scene was chaotic. The explosion was massive," said local police officer Capt. Mohamed Dahir. "Most of the victims were innocent women who were simply trying to earn a living to feed their families."

### 'They were just doing their jobs'

Witnesses described a horrific scene in the immediate aftermath of the explosion, with thick black smoke rising above the street and debris scattered across the road.

"I was standing nearby when the ground shook," said Halima Abdi, a local shopkeeper. "I ran outside and saw blood, broomsticks, and bodies on the ground. These women were just doing their jobs, cleaning the trash from our streets. It is pure cruelty."

Security forces quickly cordoned off the area to secure the site and search for secondary explosives, a common tactic used in similar attacks in the city.

No group has immediately claimed responsibility for the attack. However, Somali authorities placed the blame on Al-Shabaab, the al Qaeda-linked militant group that has waged a deadly insurgency against the Somali federal government for nearly two decades.

### A vulnerable target

Al-Shabaab has a long history of targeting municipal street cleaners in Mogadishu. The militant group often views anyone receiving a wage from the government—even low-income civic workers—as legitimate targets or spies for the administration.

Female street cleaners in Mogadishu are among the city's most vulnerable residents, often working early hours in high-risk areas for meager pay to support large households, many of them widows from Somalia’s prolonged conflict. 

Tuesday’s bombing comes amid an ongoing military campaign by the Somali government and allied clan militias aimed at driving Al-Shabaab out of its remaining strongholds in central and southern Somalia. 

While the government has made territorial gains in rural areas over the past year, the militant group continues to demonstrate its ability to carry out asymmetrical attacks, including car bombs, suicide bombings, and improvised explosive devices (IEDs) inside the capital.

Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud offered his condolences to the families of the victims in a statement Tuesday afternoon, calling the attack a "cowardly act that demonstrates the insurgents' complete disregard for human life."

Authorities say an investigation into the placement of the explosive device is underway.

**ROADSIDE BOMB KILLS 21 FEMALE STREET SWEEPERS IN MOGADISHU AMID RISING VIOLENCE**

**MOGADISHU, Somalia** — At least 21 women clearing rubbish from a major thoroughfare in Mogadishu were killed on Sunday morning when a massive roadside bomb detonated, marking one of the deadliest single attacks on civilians in the Somali capital this year. 

The victims were participating in a United Nations-backed "food-for-work" program, sweeping streets in exchange for basic food rations to support their impoverished families. The powerful blast occurred along the strategic K-4 junction road in southern Mogadishu, a frequently traveled route for government officials and allied Ethiopian military convoys.

According to witnesses, the explosion tore through a group of nearly 50 women who were gathered along the roadside carrying brooms and shovels. The force of the blast flung bodies across the road and left a crater in the asphalt.

"The scene was complete carnage," said Abdiwali Ismail, a local resident who rushed to the site shortly after the detonation. "There were bodies torn apart, mostly women who were just trying to earn food for their children. It was a horrifying sight."

### Hospitals Overwhelmed by Casualties

Local medical facilities were inundated within minutes of the blast as civilian vehicles, minibuses, and wheelbarrows rushed the wounded to emergency rooms. 

At Medina Hospital, the city’s primary medical facility, doctors reported receiving a flood of victims suffering from severe shrapnel wounds, burns, and lost limbs. 

"We have received the bodies of 15 women who died before reaching the hospital, and more than 40 other people have been admitted with critical injuries," said Dr. Mohamed Yusuf, the director of Medina Hospital. "Most of the wounded are women and children who were nearby. Our operating theaters are at full capacity, and we are desperately in need of blood donations."

Medical officials at Daynile Hospital in western Mogadishu confirmed receiving six additional dead bodies and at least a dozen injured civilians from the same explosion, bringing the total confirmed death toll to 21. Doctors expressed fear that the casualty count could rise further given the severity of the injuries.

### Political Reactions and Blame

The Transitional Federal Government (TFG) swiftly condemned the attack, calling it a "cowardly and barbaric act against innocent poor mothers." 

Senior government officials directed blame at the remnants of the Islamic Courts Union (ICU) and its radical armed wing, Al-Shabaab, which have been waging a deadly insurgency against the government and its military allies.

"This horrific attack bears the hallmark of the anti-peace elements, the Islamic Courts Union and extremist insurgents, who have no regard for human life," said Abdi Hashi, a senior official in the TFG’s Ministry of Information. "These women were targeted simply because they were working to feed their families under a program supported by the international community. The terrorists want to paralyze the city and stop any humanitarian assistance from reaching our people."

While insurgent factions frequently target military convoys using improvised explosive devices (IEDs), no group immediately claimed responsibility for Sunday’s bombing. Islamist insurgent spokesmen have previously denied deliberately targeting civilians, often blaming government forces or Ethiopian troops for indiscriminate retaliatory fire following roadside explosions. However, government security officials maintained that the bomb was intentionally planted to terrorize the civilian population and disrupt public order.

### Broader Context: Ethiopian Troops and the Djibouti Agreement

The attack underscores the volatile security environment in Somalia, where violence has metastasized since late 2006, when Ethiopian military forces intervened to help the TFG oust the Islamic Courts Union from Mogadishu and much of southern Somalia. 

Since their ousted from power, insurgent factions have waged a relentless guerrilla war using mortar attacks, targeted assassinations, and roadside bombs against Ethiopian troops, Somali government forces, and African Union peacekeepers (AMISOM). Civilians have consistently borne the brunt of the bloodshed, with hundreds of thousands displaced from Mogadishu over the past two years.

Sunday's bombing comes at a fragile political juncture. In June 2008, the TFG signed a UN-brokered peace deal in neighboring Djibouti with moderate factions of the opposition alliance, the Alliance for the Re-liberation of Somalia (ARS), led by Sheikh Sharif Sheikh Ahmed. The Djibouti Peace Agreement outlined a framework for a ceasefire, the eventual withdrawal of Ethiopian troops, and the deployment of an expanded UN peacekeeping force.

However, hardline Islamist factions—including radical leaders within the ICU and the breakaway Al-Shabaab militia—have rejected the Djibouti accord entirely. They have vowed to continue fighting until all foreign and Ethiopian troops completely withdraw from Somali soil, creating a deep rift within the opposition and fueling ongoing violence on the ground.

The attack on the humanitarian street-sweeping initiative highlights the escalating risks faced by aid operations in Somalia. International relief agencies, including the UN's World Food Programme (WFP), have warned that mounting insecurity, piracy, and direct attacks on aid workers are severely hampering efforts to respond to Somalia’s deepening humanitarian crisis, which is currently compounded by severe drought, hyperinflation, and widespread displacement.

**MOGADISHU, Somalia —** The acrid smell of burning rubber, cordite, and charred flesh hangs heavy over Maka Al Mukarama Road this evening, as rescue workers dig through the rubble of what was, just hours ago, one of Mogadishu’s most bustling commercial thoroughfares. 

At least 24 people have been confirmed dead, and more than 45 others wounded, after a massive vehicle-borne improvised explosive device (VBIED) detonated during the Tuesday evening rush hour. The attack targeted a crowded stretch of the vital artery that connects the presidential palace, Villa Somalia, to the international airport—a stretch of road long considered both the city's lifeline and its most dangerous flashpoint.

Emergency services, severely under-resourced, struggled to respond in the immediate aftermath. Ambulances navigated a labyrinth of burning vehicle carcasses and shattered concrete, their sirens drowned out by the screams of survivors and the panicked gunfire of security personnel firing into the air to clear the crowds.

### "The Ground Shook Beneath Us"

For those on the scene, the blast was instantaneous and catastrophic. 

"I was serving tea to three men outside my shop when the world turned white," said Hassan Nur, a 34-year-old street vendor whose face was dusted with dry white masonry dust. "The roar blew me backward into the store. When I crawled out, the tea stand was gone. My customers were gone. There was only fire and smoke."

At nearby Medina Hospital, the city's primary trauma center, blood stained the corridors as doctors worked frantically under flickering lights, overwhelmed by the influx of critically injured civilians.

"We are operating at three times our capacity," said Dr. Amina Dahir, her surgical scrubs soaked in blood. "Most of the victims arriving are innocent bystanders—minibus drivers, mothers returning from the market, young men drinking coffee. Many have lost limbs; others have severe third-degree burns. We are running desperately low on blood bags and basic surgical supplies."

While no group has yet officially claimed responsibility, the attack bears all the hallmarks of al-Shabaab, the Al-Qaeda-linked militant group that has waged a relentless campaign to topple the Somali state.

### A Government Drowning in Discord

The bombing comes at a moment of acute vulnerability for Somalia. Behind the fortified walls of Villa Somalia, just a mile up the road from the blast site, the country's Transitional Federal Government (TFG) is locked in a bitter, paralyzing internal feud.

For weeks, political gridlock has brought the administration to a standstill. Deep rifts between the President and the Prime Minister over cabinet appointments, security strategies, and the drafting of a new constitution have crippled governance. Key security sector reforms have stalled, leaving police and military personnel unpaid for months—a critical vulnerability that local analysts say insurgents are aggressively exploiting.

"What happened today on Maka Al Mukarama is a direct consequence of the vacuum in Villa Somalia," said a senior Western diplomat based in neighboring Nairobi, speaking on the condition of anonymity. "While the leadership of the TFG is consumed by political infighting and jockeying for power, security on the streets has completely collapsed. Al-Shabaab doesn't need to defeat the government; it just needs to wait for the government to tear itself apart."

Attempts by African Union peacekeeping forces (AMISOM) to secure key supply routes have been undermined by the lack of a cohesive national military force to hold territory. Local intelligence officials privately admit that insurgent operatives slip into the capital with alarming ease, capitalizing on compromised checkpoints and bribed guards.

### A Capital on the Edge

As night falls over Mogadishu, the silence is broken only by the occasional burst of distant gunfire and the low rumble of armored personnel carriers patrolling the darkened streets. On Maka Al Mukarama Road, shopkeepers use wooden brooms to sweep away mountainloads of shattered glass, stoic in the face of a tragedy that feels endlessly recurrent.

The TFG issued a brief statement late Tuesday condemning the "cowardly act of terror" and promising a full investigation. But for the residents of Mogadishu, who have endured decades of civil strife and political posturing, the promises ring hollow.

"They sit in their armored cars and fortified offices while we die in the streets," Hassan Nur said, looking out at the smoking crater where his livelihood used to be. "The politicians fight for power, the militants fight for God, and the rest of us just fight to stay alive until tomorrow."

**MOGADISHU, Somalia (CNN)** -- A powerful roadside bomb ripped through a group of municipal workers in Mogadishu on Sunday, killing at least 21 women who were sweeping the streets of the Somali capital, medical officials and witnesses said.

The explosion struck a busy thoroughfare in the city's southern district, where dozens of women had gathered as part of a city-sponsored cleanup initiative. The blast scattered debris across the road and left scenes of devastation in its wake.

Asha Ise Gedi, a witness who was nearby when the bomb detonated, described the horror following the explosion.

"The blast was deafening. I saw smoke rising and rushed toward the scene, but all I could see were bodies scattered across the street," Gedi said. "Most of them were poor women just trying to earn a living to feed their families. It was complete bloodbath."

The wounded were rushed to local medical facilities, primarily Medina Hospital, the city's main trauma center.

Dr. Dahir Dhere, a senior physician at Medina Hospital, confirmed the rising death toll and said the facility was overwhelmed by the influx of casualties.

"We have received 21 bodies, almost all of them women killed in the explosion," Dr. Dhere said. "Dozens of others are severely wounded with severe shrapnel injuries and burn wounds. Our medical staff is working around the clock, but our supplies are stretched to the limit."

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the bombing, though suspicion quickly fell on Islamist insurgents waging a violent campaign against Somalia's fragile Transitional Federal Government (TFG) and its supporting Ethiopian military forces. 

The attack occurs against a backdrop of severe political infighting within the upper echelons of the Somali government. A bitter rift has deepened between Prime Minister Nur Hassan Nur, widely known as "Nur Ade," and Mogadishu Mayor Mohamed Omar Habeb, known as "Mohamed Dhere."

Prime Minister Nur Ade recently issued a decree firing Mayor Mohamed Dhere, citing corruption, failure to secure the capital, and autocratic management. However, the mayor rejected his dismissal, backed by President Abdullahi Yusuf Ahmed, creating a constitutional deadlock and paralyzing local governance in Mogadishu at a time when security continues to deteriorate rapidly.

The political paralysis has left the capital increasingly vulnerable to insurgent attacks, with civilians continuing to bear the brunt of the violence.

**MOGADISHU, Somalia — October 14, 2008** — At least 14 civilians were killed and more than 30 others wounded on Tuesday morning when insurgent mortar shells struck a crowded aid distribution site in the southern district of Dharkenley, local medical officials and witnesses said.

The attack unfolded around 9:30 a.m. local time as hundreds of mothers and children lined up at a complex managed by the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) to receive monthly rations of wheat flour and vegetable oil. According to witnesses, three mortar rounds landed in rapid succession near the main entrance, sending shrapnel tearing through the crowd.

"We were standing in line waiting for our names to be called when the first explosion hit," said Amina Hassan, a mother of four who suffered minor injuries. "People began running, dropping their sacks and buckets. Then two more shells landed right among the people fleeing. It was chaos."

No group immediately claimed responsibility, but local security officials blamed Al-Shabaab, an Islamist militant organization that has waged a relentless insurgency against the country’s fragile Transitional Federal Government (TFG) and its foreign allies.

### Aid Work Under Fire

The attack underscores the extreme dangers facing civilians relying on international relief efforts in Somalia, where prolonged violence and severe drought have left an estimated 3.2 million people—nearly half the population—in need of emergency humanitarian assistance.

Following the strike, the UN agency temporarily suspended operations at three distribution points across the capital pending a security review. 

"Targeting innocent civilians who are simply trying to feed their families is a horrific violation of international humanitarian law," said a spokesperson for the UN Humanitarian Coordinator for Somalia in a statement from neighboring Kenya. "These brave aid workers and vulnerable families are paying the price for a political conflict they did not create."

Insurgent groups in Somalia have increasingly targeted UN operations and international non-governmental organizations over the past year, accusing them of serving as proxies for foreign political interests. Several high-profile aid workers have been kidnapped or assassinated in recent months, forcing many international agencies to manage operations remotely from Nairobi.

### Background of Deepening Instability

The incident comes amidst one of the most violent periods in Somalia's turbulent recent history. The current wave of instability traces back to late 2006, when Ethiopian military forces, supported by the United States, intervened to oust the Islamic Courts Union (ICU)—a alliance of Islamic judiciaries that had temporarily seized control of Mogadishu and restored a fragile order after years of warlord rule.

While the Ethiopian intervention successfully installed the UN-backed Transitional Federal Government in Mogadishu, it triggered a fierce nationalist and religious backlash. The armed wing of the ICU shattered into various insurgent factions, the most radical and potent of which emerged as Al-Shabaab.

Since 2007, Mogadishu has been transformed into an urban warzone. Insurgents employ hit-and-run tactics, roadside bombs, and targeted mortar barrages against TFG positions, Ethiopian troops, and African Union peacekeepers (AMISOM), who deployed early last year to secure key infrastructure. 

Civilians continue to bear the brunt of the violence. Shelling between insurgents launching mortars from heavily populated residential areas and government-aligned forces responding with heavy artillery has turned large swathes of Mogadishu into rubble. 

Humanitarian groups estimate that more than 800,000 people have fled Mogadishu since early 2007, creating massive squalid camps for internally displaced persons along the road to the nearby town of Afgooye.

As emergency services in Mogadishu struggled to process the victims of Tuesday's attack, local community leaders voiced growing despair over the endless cycle of violence.

"The political leaders meet in luxury hotels abroad, and the insurgents fire from our neighborhoods," said Sheikh Dahir Ahmed, a prominent elder in the Dharkenley district. "Meanwhile, the poor people who only want a bag of flour to keep their children alive are the ones who bleed in the dirt."
